passages.t: ‘Blessed is the one who cares for the poor’, and the friend who lifted his heel
passages.happening:
The heading reads, “For the choirmaster. A Psalm of David” (verse 1). The psalm begins with a blessing: “Blessed is the one who cares for the poor; the LORD will deliver him in the day of trouble” (verse 1). God will keep him even when he is sick: “The LORD will sustain him on his bed of illness” (verse 3).

Then the psalmist speaks of his own illness. “I said, ‘O LORD, be gracious to me; heal me, for I have sinned against You.’” (verse 4). His enemies wait for him to die: “When will he die and be forgotten?” (verse 5). Visitors come to his bedside and then spread gossip (verse 6).

The deepest wound is a friend. “Even my close friend whom I trusted, the one who shared my bread, has lifted up his heel against me” (verse 9).

He asks God to raise him up (verse 10), and trusts that God will set him “in Your presence forever” (verse 12).

Then the last verse is a blessing of God: “Blessed be the LORD, the God of Israel, from everlasting to everlasting. Amen and Amen” (verse 13).
passages.hearers:
‘Shared my bread’ meant more in that world than it does now. To eat with someone was to be bound to them in friendship and loyalty. To betray someone you had eaten with was a deep treachery. ‘Lifted up his heel’ is a picture of a sudden kick, or of turning your back on someone with contempt.

Many readers think of Ahithophel, David's trusted adviser, who joined his son Absalom's revolt (2 Samuel 15:12, 31). The psalm itself does not name him.

Verse 13 closes more than this psalm. It closes Book One of the Psalms, Psalms 1 to 41. Each of the first four books ends with a short blessing of God like this one (see the book page, ‘Five books’). Book Two begins with Psalm 42.
passages.later:
At the Last Supper Jesus quoted verse 9 of Judas: “But this is to fulfill the Scripture: ‘The one who shares My bread has lifted up his heel against Me.’” (John 13:18). Mark records him saying, “one of you who is eating with Me will betray Me” (Mark 14:18). John's quotation leaves out ‘whom I trusted’. Some readers think that is deliberate, since John says Jesus “had known from the beginning” who would betray him (John 6:64).

Verse 1's blessing on those who care for the poor is echoed by Jesus: “Blessed are the merciful, for they will be shown mercy” (Matthew 5:7).

The closing blessing of verse 13 returns, almost word for word, at the end of Book Four (Psalm 106:48).
passages.hard:
Verse 10 says, ‘raise me up, that I may repay them.’ Is he asking for revenge? He may mean that a king, once healed, would bring his betrayers to justice; or it may be a raw, honest wish. The book page's part on the cursing psalms sets out how Christians read such lines. Jesus, betrayed by a friend at table, still washed that friend's feet (John 13:5).

And verse 4 links his illness to his sin, as Psalm 38 does. The note on Psalm 38 says plainly that illness is not God's punishment on a reader today.
passages.asks:
Psalm 41 asks two things of you. First, care for the poor and the sick. Visit them, and do not be the visitor who gossips afterward (verse 6).

Second, if a friend has betrayed you, the psalm gives you words for that wound, and Jesus has been there before you.

And notice how Book One ends: not with the psalmist's trouble, but with ‘Amen and Amen’. Forty-one psalms of joy and tears, and the last word is praise.
